missing_spec_content.spec_text: Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never mentions spontaneous fission. It presents neutron absorption as the only route: keyPoints[0].content says "In nuclear fission, a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron". So the student is not taught that fission can occasionally happen without absorbing a neutron, or that this is rare.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says "splits into two smaller nuclei" (keyPoints[0].content) but never says the two nuclei are roughly equal in size.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[0].content says "The energy comes out as kinetic energy of the fragments and as gamma radiation", and writeBullets[4] repeats this. The released neutrons are also fission products with kinetic energy, but this is not taught. The point that all the products have kinetic energy is missing.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to draw/interpret diagrams representing nuclear fission and how a chain reaction may occur.
missing_spec_content.why: Every keyPoints[].diagram is null. The only reference is keyPoints[1].tutor_note: "Be able to draw or describe the chain reaction diagram". No fission or chain-reaction diagram is given for the student to interpret.

above_gcse.text: Each fission reaction releases about 200 MeV. A chemical reaction releases only a few eV. That is about 50 million times less.
above_gcse.why: The specification does not require MeV/eV units or energy values per reaction. These unfamiliar units could confuse the student.

above_gcse.text: ~17.6 MeV per D-T reaction, but more per kg of fuel
above_gcse.why: Specific energy values and per-kg comparisons go beyond the specification, which only says energy is released.

above_gcse.text: Moderator: this slows neutrons down to the right speed for U-235 to absorb them. It is usually water or graphite.
above_gcse.why: The specification only says "The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor". Moderators and neutron speeds are not required at this level.

above_gcse.text: They are made of boron or cadmium.
above_gcse.why: Control rod materials are not in the specification sections.

above_gcse.text: This mass difference is converted to energy by E = mc².
above_gcse.why: E = mc² is not in the specification sections. The spec only says "some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation" for fusion.
The specific deuterium–tritium reaction and its products go beyond the specification, which only defines fusion in general terms.

above_gcse.text: it needs extremely high temperatures (~100 million °C on Earth) and pressures. These overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei.
above_gcse.why: Fusion conditions, temperatures and electrostatic repulsion are not in specification section 4.4.4.2.

above_gcse.text: risk of nuclear weapons spreading, as the waste can be used for weapons
above_gcse.why: A detailed evaluation of nuclear power (proliferation, cost, named accidents, "always 30 years away") is not part of 4.4.4.1 or 4.4.4.2.

above_gcse.text: A fissile isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors; splits when it absorbs a slow neutron
above_gcse.why: The term "fissile" and the need for slow neutrons are not required by the specification.

factual_errors.text: Hydrogen isotopes used as fuel in fusion reactions; abundant and available from seawater (deuterium)
factual_errors.correction: Only deuterium is abundant and can be taken from seawater. Tritium is radioactive (half-life about 12 years) and extremely rare in nature. It has to be produced, usually from lithium, so it is not abundant.
Deuterium can be taken from seawater, but tritium cannot. D-T fusion fuel supply is limited by tritium production (from lithium). It is not simply hydrogen from seawater.

factual_errors.text: Fusion's main product is helium. Its radioactivity is much shorter-lived than that of fission fragments.
factual_errors.correction: Helium-4 is stable and not radioactive. The radioactivity linked to fusion comes from the tritium fuel and from reactor materials made radioactive by neutrons. It does not come from the helium product.

wrong_terms.text: two small nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus
wrong_terms.spec_term: the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus

wrong_terms.text: as kinetic energy of the fragments and as gamma radiation

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: 0: "In nuclear fission, what triggers a uranium-235 nucleus to split?" correct: "Absorption of a slow neutron"
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[0].content: "a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The key point content never says the neutron must be slow. "Slow" appears only in keyPoints[0].keyTerms[2].def and in the moderator part of keyPoints[1]. The answer is not fully supported by the key point it sits with.
